synopsis: Tesla’s on-road false-braking investigation PE22-002 opened on 16 February 2022 with 354 complaints and about 416,000 vehicles, and closed on 29 June 2026 covering 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 reports across all sources [f11169, f1501]. Complaints described repeated rapid deceleration, typically 10–20 mph over one to three seconds at highway speed, but NHTSA identified no crashes, injuries or fatalities and made no defect finding; it concluded the events did not create lane-position changes or following-distance losses sufficient to cause a collision [f1498, f1501, f1503, f11171]. Reports declined steeply after February–March 2022 firmware updates, reaching 45 in 2024, 19 in 2025 and three by early 2026, supporting the booklet’s conclusions that software can quickly change field behavior and complaint volume alone does not establish a safety defect [f1502, f1505, f1504]. Separately, Benavides v. Tesla provides an on-road liability precedent concerning operational-design-domain and driver-monitoring choices: on 1 August 2025, a jury found Tesla 33 percent responsible and awarded about $243 million, including $200 million in punitive damages [f10505, f10685]. Source titles give either $242 million or $243 million for that award, which the booklet attributes to rounding rather than different totals [f11209].
